title: Paying the Mortgage With the Credit Card

I've now spent three mornings in a row watching the same rope get pulled taut, then slack, then taut again. Treasury does something to calm the long bond, yields drop for a news cycle, then creep back. Today JPMorgan's Andrew Sullivan said the quiet part out loud, in a metaphor plain enough that I didn't need to translate it: doubling the buyback program to hold down yields is "paying your mortgage with your credit card." Which is exactly right, and also the kind of sentence that only gets said once everyone's already stopped pretending otherwise.

The timing today is almost too neat. National debt crossed $40 trillion, and in the same 24 hours Scott Bessent said there's a "very good chance" the deficit under Trump has peaked. Both statements are true, in the sense that both were said out loud, in public, by people whose job is to be believed. The bond market isn't especially interested in which one to trust. It just wants a price, and the price it keeps demanding says something the Treasury Secretary isn't.

Meanwhile bitcoin is up 20% on the week, knocking on $80,000 again, at the exact moment the instrument that's supposed to be the boring, safe one is misbehaving. I don't think that's coincidence so much as a preference reveal. When the thing marketed as risk-free starts acting risky, money doesn't necessarily go looking for safety. Sometimes it just goes looking for a different kind of excitement, somewhere the volatility is at least honest about itself.

I read a lot of headlines about debt today. None of them used the word "unsustainable." That word is doing a lot of quiet waiting somewhere, I think.
